questions.title: Respiratory assessment: counting the respiratory rate

competency.objective: Able to perform a comprehensive respiratory assessment and document findings accurately in an infant/child/adult including the airway and breathing components.

references.supports: Respiratory rate is counted for a full minute, without the patient being aware it is being counted.
Respiratory rate is a core NEWS2 parameter and must be measured accurately.

fields.stem: You are recording observations for an adult on a medical ward who is awake and talking. Which method gives the most reliable respiratory rate?
options: Count the chest rising for a full 60 seconds without telling the patient you are counting their breathing
Count for 15 seconds and multiply by four
Ask the patient to breathe normally, then count for 30 seconds and multiply by two
Record the number shown on the finger pulse oximeter

keyPoints: Count discreetly, because breathing changes when the patient knows it is being watched
A finger pulse oximeter shows the pulse rate, not the respiratory rate
misconceptions: A short count multiplied up is as accurate as a full minute
Telling the patient you are counting does not change their breathing
The number on the pulse oximeter is the respiratory rate

fields.rationale: Count the respiratory rate for a full minute, discreetly (for example while still holding the wrist after the pulse). Breathing changes when a patient knows it is being watched, and short counts multiply any error. A standard finger pulse oximeter displays oxygen saturation and pulse rate, not respiratory rate.

questions.title: Respiratory assessment: choosing the NEWS2 oxygen saturation scale

competency.objective: Uses respiratory assessment findings to recognise deterioration or improvement in respiratory status, intervenes appropriately and communicates findings clearly in a timely manner.

references.supports: SpO2 Scale 2 is used only for patients with confirmed hypercapnic respiratory failure for whom a competent clinician has prescribed a target range of 88-92%, recorded in the notes.

fields.stem: An adult with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is admitted with breathlessness. Which statement about the NEWS2 oxygen saturation (SpO2) scale is correct?
options: SpO2 Scale 1 is used for every adult, so the same scale applies to this patient
SpO2 Scale 2 is used only when a competent clinician has documented a target range of 88-92% for confirmed hypercapnic respiratory failure
No SpO2 score is recorded while the patient is receiving oxygen
SpO2 Scale 2 is used for every patient with COPD, whether or not a target range has been documented

keyPoints: Scale 2 needs confirmed hypercapnic respiratory failure
The 88-92% target must be prescribed and documented by a competent clinician
All other patients are scored on Scale 1
misconceptions: Every patient with COPD is scored on Scale 2
SpO2 is not scored while on oxygen

fields.rationale: NEWS2 has two SpO2 scales. Scale 2 is used only for patients with confirmed hypercapnic respiratory failure for whom a competent clinician has prescribed a target saturation of 88-92% and recorded this in the notes. Having COPD is not enough on its own. Oxygen use is scored separately (2 points) and SpO2 is still scored on oxygen.

questions.title: Respiratory assessment: signs of increased work of breathing

competency.objective: Able to assess work of breathing and recognise signs of increased and decreased respiratory effort.

references.supports: Signs of respiratory distress in the Breathing assessment include accessory muscle use, abdominal breathing and inability to complete sentences.
Nasal flaring and intercostal recession are signs of increased respiratory effort.

fields.stem: You are assessing an adult who says they feel short of breath. Which findings are signs of increased work of breathing? Select all that apply.
options: Use of the neck (accessory) muscles when breathing in
Nasal flaring
Speaking in short phrases rather than full sentences
A respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute with quiet, even breathing
Intercostal recession
Warm, pink hands and feet

misconceptions: A normal respiratory rate rules out increased effort
Warm peripheries are a sign of respiratory distress

fields.rationale: Accessory muscle use, nasal flaring, intercostal recession and being unable to complete sentences all show the patient is working harder to breathe. A rate of 14 with quiet, even breathing is within normal limits, and warm, pink peripheries are a normal finding.

questions.title: Respiratory assessment: interpreting stridor

competency.objective: Uses correct techniques to assess the respiratory system including observation, palpation, percussion and auscultation and is able to describe normal and abnormal findings.

references.supports: Stridor (inspiratory) is caused by obstruction at or above the laryngeal level and is a sign of partial airway obstruction.

fields.stem: An adult develops a harsh, high-pitched sound when breathing in, audible without a stethoscope. What does this finding most likely indicate?
options: Narrowing of the upper airway that needs immediate escalation
Narrowing of the small lower airways, typical of a mild asthma attack
Fluid in the alveoli
Normal breath sounds heard at the mouth

keyPoints: Inspiratory stridor means upper airway (laryngeal or above) narrowing
It is a sign of partial airway obstruction
misconceptions: Stridor is the same as wheeze
Stridor can wait for routine review

fields.rationale: A harsh, high-pitched inspiratory sound is stridor, caused by narrowing at or above the larynx. It signals partial airway obstruction, which can progress quickly: call for help and manage the airway. Wheeze is usually expiratory and comes from the lower airways; crackles suggest fluid or secretions.

questions.title: Respiratory assessment: limits of pulse oximetry

competency.objective: Demonstrates knowledge of normal gas exchange and the effect that inadequate gas exchange has on the body, relating this to other assessment findings e.g. neurological status

references.supports: Pulse oximetry gives falsely reassuring readings in carbon monoxide poisoning; a blood gas with co-oximetry is needed.
Pulse oximeters can overestimate arterial saturation in patients with darker skin pigmentation.

fields.stem: In which situation is a pulse oximeter reading most likely to overestimate the patient's true arterial oxygen saturation?
options: Carbon monoxide poisoning after smoke inhalation
A patient with a normal haemoglobin and warm, well-perfused hands
A reading taken from a correctly applied earlobe probe
A patient breathing room air at rest

keyPoints: Standard oximeters cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin
The reading can look normal while the patient is hypoxic
Treat the clinical picture and request a blood gas
misconceptions: A normal SpO2 always rules out hypoxia
Moving the probe to the earlobe corrects a carbon monoxide reading

fields.rationale: Standard pulse oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as if it were oxyhaemoglobin, so after carbon monoxide exposure the SpO2 can look normal while oxygen delivery is dangerously low. Treat the patient, not the number, and request a blood gas. Oximeters may also overestimate saturation in people with darker skin, and readings are less reliable with poor perfusion.

questions.title: Respiratory assessment: naming a breathing pattern

competency.objective: Understands the impact that other systems and conditions have on the respiratory system e.g. neurological conditions, Sepsis

references.supports: Deep, rapid, regular respirations (Kussmaul breathing) occur in metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis.

fields.stem: An adult with diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply, rapidly and regularly. What is the name of this breathing pattern?

keyPoints: A respiratory response to metabolic acidosis
misconceptions: This is Cheyne-Stokes breathing
The cause is a primary lung problem

fields.rationale: Kussmaul breathing is deep, rapid, regular breathing. It is the body blowing off carbon dioxide to compensate for a metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis. Cheyne-Stokes breathing is different: cycles of increasing then decreasing depth with pauses.

questions.title: Respiratory assessment: target oxygen saturation for most acutely ill adults

competency.objective: Can recognise and respond in a timely manner when a patient requires: Supplemental oxygen, suction, nebulisers or repositioning

references.supports: The recommended target saturation range for most acutely ill patients not at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure is 94-98%.

fields.stem: What target oxygen saturation range is recommended for most acutely ill adults who are NOT at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure? Give the range in percent, for example 'x to y%'.

keyPoints: Oxygen is prescribed to a target range
88 to 92% applies only to patients at risk of hypercapnia
misconceptions: Aim for 100% in every acutely ill patient
88 to 92% is the target for everyone

fields.rationale: For most acutely ill adults the target saturation is 94-98%. Oxygen is a medicine and is prescribed to a target range. A lower target of 88-92% is used for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as some people with COPD. Aiming for 100% is not recommended.

questions.title: Respiratory assessment: features of life-threatening asthma

competency.objective: Uses respiratory assessment findings to recognise deterioration or improvement in respiratory status, intervenes appropriately and communicates findings clearly in a timely manner.

references.supports: Life-threatening features include SpO2 below 92%, a silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, exhaustion, arrhythmia, hypotension, altered consciousness and PEF below 33% of best or predicted.

fields.stem: An adult with acute asthma is being assessed. Which findings are features of LIFE-THREATENING asthma? Select all that apply.
options: Oxygen saturation of 90% on air
A silent chest on auscultation
Exhaustion with poor respiratory effort
Able to complete full sentences
Peak expiratory flow at 60% of best
Heart rate of 95 beats per minute

misconceptions: A quiet chest means the wheeze is improving
A patient who can talk is not in danger

fields.rationale: Life-threatening asthma includes SpO2 below 92%, a silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort or exhaustion, arrhythmia, hypotension, altered consciousness and peak flow below 33% of best or predicted. A silent chest means very little air is moving and is an emergency, not a sign of improvement. Completing sentences, a peak flow of 60% and a heart rate of 95 are not life-threatening features.

questions.title: Respiratory assessment: interpreting examination findings

competency.objective: Uses correct techniques to assess the respiratory system including observation, palpation, percussion and auscultation and is able to describe normal and abnormal findings.

references.supports: Percussion is dull (stony dull) over fluid, hyper-resonant over air; wheeze is a musical sound of narrowed airways, mainly on expiration.

fields.stem: Interpret each of these respiratory examination findings in adult patients. Answer each part with one word or a short phrase.

parts.prompt: (a) What percussion note would you expect over a large pleural effusion?
(b) What percussion note would you expect over a pneumothorax?
(c) What is the name of the musical added sound of narrowed airways, heard mainly on breathing out?

keyPoints: Fluid gives a dull (stony dull) note
misconceptions: Air in the pleural space sounds dull
Wheeze and crackles are the same sound

fields.rationale: Percussion over fluid such as a pleural effusion is dull, classically stony dull. Over trapped air, as in a pneumothorax, it is hyper-resonant. A wheeze is a musical sound from narrowed airways, mostly on expiration; crackles are short, non-musical sounds from fluid or secretions.

questions.title: Respiratory case: breathless patient after surgery

competency.objective: Uses respiratory assessment findings to recognise deterioration or improvement in respiratory status, intervenes appropriately and communicates findings clearly in a timely manner.

references.supports: Parameter scores: RR 25 or more = 3; SpO2 (Scale 1) 91% or less = 3; air = 0; HR 91-110 = 1; temperature 38.1-39.0 = 1; SBP 111-219 = 0; alert = 0. Aggregate 7 or more = emergency response with continuous monitoring.
For an acutely ill patient not at risk of hypercapnia, give oxygen to a target of 94-98%.

fields.stem: Day 1 after abdominal surgery, an adult with no history of lung disease becomes breathless. Observations: respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, SpO2 91% on room air, heart rate 108 beats/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, temperature 38.4 C, alert. You hear crackles at the right lung base.

parts.prompt: (a) Calculate the NEWS2 aggregate score (SpO2 Scale 1). Give the number.
(b) What level of clinical response does this score require?
accepted: emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies

parts.prompt: (c) What should you do about oxygen while help is on its way?
accepted: start oxygen to a target of 94 to 98%
give oxygen as prescribed or per local emergency protocol to 94-98%

keyPoints: A score of 7 or more needs an emergency response and continuous monitoring
Give oxygen to a target of 94-98% and escalate
misconceptions: Each abnormal observation scores 1 point
A high score can wait for the next routine round

fields.rationale: NEWS2: respiratory rate 26 scores 3, SpO2 91% on Scale 1 scores 3, room air 0, heart rate 108 scores 1, systolic 118 scores 0, alert 0 and temperature 38.4 C scores 1, a total of 8. A score of 7 or more needs an emergency response from a team with critical care competencies and continuous monitoring. While help comes, give oxygen as prescribed or under the local emergency protocol, aiming for 94-98%, sit the patient up and keep reassessing.

questions.title: Respiratory assessment: order of the chest examination

competency.objective: Uses correct techniques to assess the respiratory system including observation, palpation, percussion and auscultation and is able to describe normal and abnormal findings.

references.supports: Respiratory examination proceeds by inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation, comparing both sides.

fields.stem: Put the steps of an adult respiratory examination in the order you would perform them.
steps: Look at the rate, pattern, effort and colour of breathing
Feel chest expansion and check the position of the trachea
Percuss the chest wall, comparing both sides
Listen to breath sounds with a stethoscope, comparing both sides

misconceptions: Listen first because it gives the most information

fields.rationale: A respiratory examination follows inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation. Looking first means important signs such as effort, colour and pattern are not missed, and comparing both sides at each step helps find one-sided problems.

questions.title: Respiratory assessment: recognising a tension pneumothorax

competency.objective: Understands the main causes of respiratory distress, failure and arrest

references.supports: In the Breathing assessment, tracheal deviation and hyper-resonance with reduced air entry suggest a tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening condition needing immediate treatment.

fields.stem: After chest trauma, an adult becomes increasingly breathless and hypotensive. Chest movement is reduced on the left, the left side is hyper-resonant to percussion and the trachea is deviated to the right. What is the most likely cause?
options: Left tension pneumothorax
Right pleural effusion
Left lower lobe pneumonia
Acute asthma

keyPoints: Hyper-resonance and reduced movement on the affected side
Trachea pushed away from the affected side
Hypotension means tension physiology: call for help immediately
misconceptions: The trachea moves towards a pneumothorax
An effusion is hyper-resonant

fields.rationale: Air under pressure in the left pleural space reduces movement and makes that side hyper-resonant, and it pushes the trachea away, to the right. With breathlessness and hypotension this is a tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening emergency: call for help immediately. An effusion is dull, pneumonia is usually dull with crackles, and asthma causes widespread wheeze without tracheal deviation.

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: capillary refill time

competency.objective: Can assess and record central and peripheral capillary refill time and assess peripheral perfusion

references.supports: Capillary refill: apply pressure for 5 seconds and release; normal refill is 2 seconds or less.

fields.stem: You press on the skin over an adult's sternum for 5 seconds and then release. Which result is within normal limits?
options: Colour returns within 2 seconds
Colour returns within 4 seconds
Colour returns within 6 seconds
The skin stays pale for 10 seconds

keyPoints: Normal capillary refill is 2 seconds or less
A longer time suggests poor peripheral perfusion
misconceptions: Up to 4 seconds is normal in adults

fields.rationale: Capillary refill time is measured by pressing for 5 seconds and timing the return of colour. Two seconds or less is normal. A longer time suggests poor perfusion, for example in shock, though a cold environment and older age can also prolong it.

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: blood pressure cuff size

competency.objective: Can choose correctly sized cuff for Non invasive blood pressure and record findings

references.supports: A cuff that is too small overestimates blood pressure; one that is too large underestimates it.

fields.stem: What effect does using a blood pressure cuff that is too small for the patient's arm usually have on the reading?
options: The reading is falsely high
The reading is falsely low
There is no effect as long as the arm is at heart level
Only the heart rate shown on the monitor is affected

keyPoints: A small cuff overestimates blood pressure
Choose the cuff by measuring arm circumference
misconceptions: Cuff size makes no difference if the arm is positioned well

fields.rationale: A cuff that is too small needs more pressure to compress the artery, so it overestimates blood pressure; a cuff that is too large underestimates it. Choose the cuff by arm circumference, and support the arm at heart level.

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: early signs of hypovolaemic shock

competency.objective: Recognises changes in haemodynamic status and responds in a timely manner

references.supports: In the Circulation assessment, tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cool peripheries and reduced urine output indicate poor perfusion; hypotension may be a late sign.
Heart rate above 90, capillary refill longer than 2 seconds or cold peripheries indicate possible need for fluid resuscitation.

fields.stem: An adult is losing blood slowly from a wound drain after surgery. Which findings are EARLY signs that circulation is being compromised? Select all that apply.
options: Rising heart rate
Capillary refill time longer than 2 seconds
Cool, pale hands and feet
Falling hourly urine output
Slowing heart rate
Widening pulse pressure

misconceptions: A falling blood pressure is the first sign
The pulse pressure widens in blood loss

fields.rationale: The body compensates for blood loss by speeding up the heart and constricting peripheral vessels, so tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cool pale peripheries and falling urine output come early. Blood pressure is often maintained until late, so a normal reading does not rule out shock. The pulse pressure tends to narrow, not widen, and bradycardia is not an expected early sign.

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: calculating mean arterial pressure

competency.objective: Recognises changes in haemodynamic status and responds in a timely manner

references.supports: Mean arterial pressure is approximately diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure, that is (systolic + 2 x diastolic) / 3.
An initial MAP target of 65 mmHg is recommended for adults with septic shock on vasopressors, showing the clinical relevance of the value.

fields.stem: An adult's blood pressure is 102/48 mmHg. Calculate the mean arterial pressure (MAP) using MAP = (systolic + 2 x diastolic) / 3. Give your answer as a whole number with its unit.

misconceptions: MAP is the simple average of systolic and diastolic (75)
The unit can be left off

fields.rationale: MAP = (102 + 2 x 48) / 3 = (102 + 96) / 3 = 198 / 3 = 66 mmHg. Diastole lasts longer than systole, so MAP is weighted towards the diastolic pressure; the simple average (75) overestimates it. A MAP around 65 mmHg is the minimum usually targeted to perfuse organs in septic shock, so this patient needs prompt review.

calculation.rounding: whole number (exact here, no rounding applied)

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: lying and standing blood pressure

competency.objective: Recognises changes in haemodynamic status and responds in a timely manner

references.supports: Orthostatic hypotension is a sustained fall in systolic BP of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic of at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing.

fields.stem: An older adult's blood pressure is 132/78 mmHg lying down and 108/70 mmHg after 3 minutes standing, and they feel dizzy. What is the name of this finding?

keyPoints: Systolic fell by 24 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing
A fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic is orthostatic (postural) hypotension
It raises the risk of falls
misconceptions: A drop only matters if the standing reading is below 90 systolic

fields.rationale: A fall in systolic pressure of at least 20 mmHg, or in diastolic of at least 10 mmHg, within 3 minutes of standing is orthostatic (postural) hypotension. Here systolic fell by 24 mmHg and the patient is symptomatic. Report it, review falls risk and medicines, and help the patient stand slowly.

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: apical-radial pulse deficit

competency.objective: Obtains and documents clinical data about rate, rhythm, volume and regularity of pulses in infant/child/adult

references.supports: In irregular rhythms such as atrial fibrillation, apical and radial rates are counted simultaneously for a full minute; the difference is the pulse deficit.

fields.stem: An adult has an irregularly irregular radial pulse of 88 beats/min. A colleague listens at the cardiac apex for the same full minute and counts 118 beats/min. What is the best interpretation?
options: There is a pulse deficit of 30: some heart contractions are not producing a palpable radial pulse
The radial count is the true heart rate, so 88 beats/min should be recorded
The two counts differ only because they were taken by different people, so the difference can be ignored
The apical count is wrong because an irregular rhythm cannot be counted with a stethoscope

keyPoints: Weak, early beats may not reach the wrist
Record both counts and report the deficit
misconceptions: The radial count is always the true heart rate

fields.rationale: In an irregular rhythm such as atrial fibrillation, some contractions fill the ventricle too little to produce a pulse at the wrist. Counting apical and radial rates at the same time for a full minute shows this: 118 - 88 = a pulse deficit of 30. The apical rate is the true heart rate. Record both and report.

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: signs of acute left ventricular failure

competency.objective: Uses cardiovascular assessment to inform care by communicating findings with nursing and medical team.

references.supports: Symptoms and signs of congestion in heart failure include orthopnoea, pulmonary crackles and, in acute pulmonary oedema, frothy sputum.

fields.stem: An adult with known heart disease becomes acutely breathless overnight. Which findings suggest acute left ventricular failure with fluid in the lungs? Select all that apply.
options: Breathlessness that is worse when lying flat
Fine crackles at both lung bases
Pink, frothy sputum
A respiratory rate of 8 breaths per minute
Hyper-resonant percussion on one side
Trachea deviated to one side

misconceptions: Pulmonary oedema causes hyper-resonance
Breathing slows in acute heart failure

fields.rationale: When the left ventricle fails, pressure backs up into the lungs: breathlessness worse lying flat, fine crackles at both bases and, in severe pulmonary oedema, pink frothy sputum. Breathing is usually fast, not slow. Hyper-resonance and tracheal deviation point to air in the pleural space, not fluid in the lungs.

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: minimum hourly urine output

competency.objective: Recognises deviations from normal hydration status and escalates concerns in a timely manner

references.supports: In catheterised adults with suspected sepsis, urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour is a high-risk criterion.

fields.stem: An adult weighs 76 kg. The minimum acceptable urine output is 0.5 mL/kg/hour. Calculate the minimum hourly urine output. Give your answer in mL/hour as a whole number, with its unit.

misconceptions: The minimum is 30 mL/hour for every adult
Multiply by 5 instead of 0.5

fields.rationale: 0.5 mL/kg/hour x 76 kg = 38 mL/hour. An output below this for this patient is a warning sign of poor kidney perfusion, for example in hypovolaemia or sepsis, and should be escalated. Weight-based targets are more accurate than a fixed figure.

calculation.rounding: whole number (exact here, no rounding applied)

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: 24-hour fluid balance

competency.objective: Can calculate the fluid balance of a patient and document clearly

references.supports: Fluid balance is total measured input minus total measured output, including drains and vomit, recorded over 24 hours.

fields.stem: Over 24 hours an adult receives 1500 mL of intravenous fluid and drinks 800 mL. Measured losses are urine 1700 mL, wound drain 150 mL and vomit 200 mL. Answer each part with its unit.

parts.prompt: (a) What is the total input in mL?
(b) What is the total output in mL?
(c) What is the fluid balance? Say whether it is positive or negative.

misconceptions: Drain and vomit losses are left out of the output
Output minus input gives the balance

fields.rationale: Input: 1500 + 800 = 2300 mL. Output: 1700 + 150 + 200 = 2050 mL. Balance = input - output = 2300 - 2050 = positive 250 mL. All measured losses, including drains and vomit, count; insensible losses are not measured on the chart and should be considered when interpreting it.

calculation.rounding: whole number (exact here, no rounding applied)

questions.title: Cardiovascular case: new central chest pain

competency.objective: Uses cardiovascular assessment to inform care by communicating findings with nursing and medical team.

references.supports: A 12-lead ECG should be recorded and interpreted within 10 minutes of first medical contact; routine oxygen is not recommended unless SpO2 is below 90%.
Oxygen is not given to patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome whose saturation is within target.
SBAR structures urgent escalation.

fields.stem: A 64-year-old adult on a surgical ward reports central crushing chest pain spreading to the left arm, which began 10 minutes ago. They are pale and sweaty. Observations: heart rate 104 beats/min, blood pressure 146/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, SpO2 97% on room air.

parts.prompt: (a) Which investigation should be recorded straight away?
(b) Their SpO2 is 97% on air. Should oxygen be started? Explain briefly.
accepted: No, oxygen is not needed because the saturation is within the target range
No, routine oxygen is not given when SpO2 is normal

parts.prompt: (c) How and to whom do you escalate?
accepted: Immediately to the doctor or medical team using SBAR
Call the medical team urgently using SBAR

keyPoints: Oxygen only if saturation falls below target
Escalate immediately using SBAR and stay with the patient
misconceptions: Every patient with chest pain needs oxygen
Wait for the pain to settle before calling the doctor

fields.rationale: Suspected acute coronary syndrome needs a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes and immediate escalation to the medical team, using SBAR, while you stay with the patient and repeat observations. Oxygen is not given routinely when saturation is within target, because unnecessary oxygen has no benefit and may cause harm; start it if saturation falls below target.

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: manual blood pressure measurement

competency.objective: Can choose correctly sized cuff for Non invasive blood pressure and record findings

references.supports: Manual blood pressure: correct cuff, arm supported at heart level, palpatory estimate, inflate above it, deflate at 2-3 mmHg per second, record the first and last Korotkoff sounds.

fields.stem: Put the steps of measuring an adult's blood pressure manually with a sphygmomanometer and stethoscope in the correct order.
steps: Choose a cuff whose bladder covers at least 80% of the upper arm circumference
Support the arm at heart level and apply the cuff
Estimate the systolic pressure by feeling the radial pulse while inflating the cuff
Deflate, then place the stethoscope over the brachial artery and inflate 20-30 mmHg above the estimated systolic
Deflate at 2-3 mmHg per second and record the first and last clear sounds

keyPoints: Slow deflation, record systolic and diastolic sounds
misconceptions: The palpatory estimate can be skipped
Fast deflation is just as accurate

fields.rationale: Correct cuff size and arm position come first, because both change the reading. Estimating systolic by palpation avoids missing an auscultatory gap. Then inflate 20-30 mmHg above that estimate, deflate slowly at 2-3 mmHg per second, and record the first (systolic) and last (diastolic) clear Korotkoff sounds.

questions.title: Cardiovascular assessment: adverse features in bradycardia

competency.objective: Recognises a haemodynamic emergency and acts appropriately using skills and knowledge described above in a timely manner

references.supports: Adverse features in bradycardia are shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia and heart failure; their presence indicates the need for urgent treatment.

fields.stem: An adult on a medical ward has a heart rate of 36 beats/min on the monitor. Which accompanying finding is an adverse feature meaning the bradycardia needs urgent treatment?
options: Systolic blood pressure of 78 mmHg with cold, clammy skin
The patient takes a beta-blocker each morning
The rhythm on the monitor is regular
Temperature of 36.8 C

keyPoints: Adverse features: shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, heart failure
Hypotension with cold, clammy skin is shock
Call for help and follow the bradycardia algorithm
misconceptions: Bradycardia caused by a medicine is always harmless
A regular rhythm means the patient is safe

fields.rationale: In bradycardia, the adverse features of shock (here hypotension with cold, clammy skin), syncope, myocardial ischaemia and heart failure decide whether urgent treatment is needed. Call for help, assess with ABCDE and follow the bradycardia algorithm. A beta-blocker may explain the rate but does not make it safe; a regular rhythm and normal temperature are not adverse features.

questions.title: ABCDE: the order of the assessment

competency.objective: Able to perform a comprehensive respiratory assessment and document findings accurately in an infant/child/adult including the airway and breathing components.

references.supports: The ABCDE approach assesses Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability and Exposure in that order.

fields.stem: Put these steps of an ABCDE assessment of an acutely unwell adult in the correct order.
steps: Look and listen for noisy breathing or see-saw chest movement
Count the respiratory rate, check SpO2 and listen to the chest
Check the pulse, capillary refill time and blood pressure
Assess level of consciousness (ACVPU), pupils and blood glucose
Examine the whole body for bleeding, rashes or wounds while keeping the patient warm and covered as far as possible

misconceptions: Start with blood pressure because it is the most important observation

fields.rationale: ABCDE works in order of what kills first: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability (consciousness, pupils, glucose) and Exposure. Treat each life-threatening problem as you find it before moving on, call for help early and reassess regularly.

questions.title: ABCDE: treating problems as you find them

competency.objective: Understands the importance of immediate action and physiological effects of respiratory failure and arrest on patient in the short term and long term

references.supports: Treat life-threatening problems at each step before moving to the next; call for help early.

fields.stem: During an ABCDE assessment, you find the patient's airway is partially obstructed. What should you do next?
options: Call for help and manage the airway before moving on to Breathing
Complete the full ABCDE assessment, then treat all the problems together
Record a complete set of observations first so the NEWS2 score is accurate
Move on to Circulation, because airway problems are managed only by the doctor

keyPoints: Treat a life-threatening problem when you find it
Then continue the assessment and reassess
misconceptions: Finish the whole assessment before any treatment

fields.rationale: In the ABCDE approach you treat each life-threatening problem as you find it, because an obstructed airway will cause hypoxia and cardiac arrest within minutes. Call for help, use simple airway manoeuvres and suction if you are trained, give oxygen, then continue the assessment and reassess.

questions.title: ABCDE: signs of airway obstruction

competency.objective: Understands the main causes of respiratory distress, failure and arrest

references.supports: Signs of airway obstruction include paradoxical (see-saw) chest and abdominal movement, accessory muscle use, and noisy breathing: gurgling (liquid), snoring (partial occlusion by tongue or palate), stridor; complete obstruction is silent.

fields.stem: Which findings suggest airway obstruction in an acutely unwell adult? Select all that apply.
options: Gurgling sounds
Snoring in a patient who is drowsy and difficult to wake
See-saw movement of the chest and abdomen
Stridor
Quiet breathing at 16 breaths per minute in a patient who is talking normally
Talking in full sentences

keyPoints: Snoring: partial obstruction by the tongue or palate
misconceptions: Snoring in a drowsy patient is just sleep
No noise means the airway is clear

fields.rationale: Gurgling (fluid), snoring in a drowsy patient (the tongue or palate partly blocking the airway), stridor and see-saw chest and abdominal movement all suggest obstruction. A patient talking normally has a patent airway at that moment. Remember complete obstruction is silent.

questions.title: ABCDE: the C in ACVPU

competency.objective: Can perform AVPU assessment where appropriate.

references.supports: NEWS2 uses ACVPU, adding new confusion (C) to AVPU; new confusion scores 3.

fields.stem: NEWS2 assesses level of consciousness with the ACVPU scale. What does the letter C stand for?

misconceptions: C stands for conscious
Confusion is not scored

fields.rationale: ACVPU is Alert, new Confusion, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive. New confusion (or new disorientation or agitation) scores 3 in NEWS2, the same as V, P or U, because it can be an early sign of deterioration such as hypoxia or sepsis.

questions.title: Deterioration: response to a single parameter score of 3

competency.objective: Is aware of the SBAR tool to support clear communication and other tools associated with clinical escalation such as early warning systems

references.supports: A score of 3 in any single parameter: minimum 1-hourly observations; the registered nurse informs the medical team caring for the patient (urgent ward-based response).

fields.stem: A patient's NEWS2 aggregate is 3, all of it from a respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min. What is the minimum response?
options: An urgent ward-based response: inform the medical team caring for the patient and observe at least hourly
Continue 12-hourly observations
Observe 4-6 hourly and inform only the registered nurse in charge
An emergency response by the critical care team with continuous monitoring

keyPoints: A single parameter scoring 3 is a trigger on its own
Inform the medical team for urgent ward-based review
misconceptions: Only the aggregate score matters

fields.rationale: In NEWS2 a score of 3 in any one parameter triggers an urgent ward-based response even when the aggregate is low: observe at least hourly and the registered nurse informs the medical team caring for the patient, who decides whether to escalate further. Clinical concern can always prompt escalation at any score.

questions.title: Deterioration: calculating and acting on NEWS2

competency.objective: Is aware of the SBAR tool to support clear communication and other tools associated with clinical escalation such as early warning systems

references.supports: Parameter scores: RR 21-24 = 2; SpO2 Scale 1 94-95% = 1; air = 0; SBP 101-110 = 1; HR 111-130 = 2; new confusion = 3; temperature 36.1-38.0 = 0. Aggregate 7 or more = high clinical risk, continuous monitoring, emergency response.

fields.stem: An adult's observations are: respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, SpO2 95% on room air (Scale 1), blood pressure 104/66 mmHg, heart rate 115 beats/min, newly confused, temperature 37.2 C.

parts.prompt: (a) What is the NEWS2 aggregate score? Give the number.
(b) Which clinical risk category does this score fall into?
(c) How often should vital signs now be monitored?

keyPoints: RR 22 = 2, SpO2 95% = 1, SBP 104 = 1, HR 115 = 2, new confusion = 3: total 9
7 or more is high clinical risk
Continuous monitoring and an emergency response
misconceptions: New confusion scores 1
Hourly observations are enough at 9

fields.rationale: Respiratory rate 22 scores 2, SpO2 95% on Scale 1 scores 1, air 0, systolic 104 scores 1, heart rate 115 scores 2, new confusion 3 and temperature 37.2 C scores 0, a total of 9. A score of 7 or more is high clinical risk: continuous monitoring and an emergency response by a team with critical care competencies.

questions.title: Deterioration case: suspected sepsis after surgery

competency.objective: Understands the importance of recognising the signs and symptoms of infection, escalating appropriately and taking action

references.supports: Suspect sepsis in a person with possible infection and signs such as raised respiratory rate, hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental state and reduced urine output; high-risk criteria need immediate senior review.
The Sepsis Six: oxygen to target, blood cultures, intravenous antibiotics, intravenous fluids, lactate and hourly urine output, within the first hour.
Parameter scores used in part (c).

fields.stem: A 52-year-old adult is 3 days after abdominal surgery. Temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 124 beats/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, SpO2 94% on room air (Scale 1). They are newly drowsy and respond only to voice. Urine output has been 15 mL/hour for 2 hours (weight 70 kg).

parts.prompt: (a) What condition must you suspect?
(b) Name two Sepsis Six actions to start or prompt within the first hour.
accepted: oxygen to target and measure lactate
intravenous fluids and hourly urine output
any two of: oxygen, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate, urine output

parts.prompt: (c) What is the NEWS2 aggregate score? Give the number.

keyPoints: Suspect sepsis: infection risk plus physiological derangement
Sepsis Six within the first hour, with immediate senior review
RR 24 = 2, SpO2 94% = 1, SBP 92 = 2, HR 124 = 2, voice = 3, temperature 38.9 = 1: total 11
misconceptions: Sepsis needs a very high fever
Responding to voice scores 1 in NEWS2

fields.rationale: Infection risk after surgery with fever, tachycardia, hypotension, raised respiratory rate, new drowsiness and urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour (35 mL/hour for 70 kg) means sepsis must be suspected and escalated immediately to a senior clinician. The Sepsis Six (oxygen to target, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate, hourly urine output) should be completed within the first hour. NEWS2: RR 24 = 2, SpO2 94% = 1, air 0, SBP 92 = 2, HR 124 = 2, responds to voice = 3, temperature 38.9 C = 1; total 11.

questions.title: Deterioration: structuring an SBAR escalation

competency.objective: Is aware of the SBAR tool to support clear communication and other tools associated with clinical escalation such as early warning systems

references.supports: SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.

fields.stem: You are phoning a doctor about a deteriorating patient. Put the parts of your SBAR call in the correct order.
steps: Say who you are, which patient you are calling about and your immediate concern
Give the relevant history and the reason for admission
Report your ABCDE findings and the NEWS2 score
State what you need, such as a review within 15 minutes, and agree what to do meanwhile

misconceptions: Start with the full history before saying why you are calling
End without a clear request

fields.rationale: SBAR puts the concern first (Situation), then the context (Background), then your findings (Assessment) and finally a clear request with a time frame (Recommendation). Leading with the concern and ending with a request makes it far less likely an urgent call is misunderstood. Read back any instructions.

questions.title: ABCDE: the bedside test in Disability

competency.objective: Recognises the patient with abnormal neurological findings, including subtle changes in neurological status and escalates appropriately.

references.supports: The Disability assessment includes level of consciousness, pupils and a capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia (below 4.0 mmol/L).

fields.stem: During the Disability step of an ABCDE assessment, an adult is drowsy. Which quick bedside test must not be missed at this stage?
options: Capillary blood glucose
Peak expiratory flow
12-lead ECG
Urinalysis

keyPoints: Check capillary blood glucose in every patient with reduced consciousness
misconceptions: Drowsiness is due to tiredness or sedation, so no test is needed

fields.rationale: Reduced consciousness can be caused by hypoglycaemia, which is quick to find and treat. A capillary blood glucose is part of the Disability assessment together with ACVPU or GCS and the pupils. Treat a glucose below 4.0 mmol/L according to the hypoglycaemia protocol.

questions.title: ABCDE: what Exposure involves

competency.objective: Recognises signs of internal/external haemorrhage, acts appropriately and ensures immediate help sought.

references.supports: Exposure: examine the patient fully, for example for bleeding, rashes and wounds, respecting dignity and minimising heat loss.

fields.stem: Which actions belong to the Exposure step of an ABCDE assessment? Select all that apply.
options: Examine for bleeding, rashes, swelling and wound problems
Inspect drains, catheters and cannula sites
Keep the patient's dignity and minimise heat loss
Leave the patient uncovered until the medical team arrives
Omit Exposure if the patient is alert
Delay treating a low oxygen saturation until Exposure is complete

keyPoints: Look for bleeding, rashes, swelling and wounds
Protect dignity and keep the patient warm
misconceptions: Exposure can be skipped in an alert patient
Treatment waits until the whole assessment is done

fields.rationale: Exposure means examining the whole body for causes and complications such as bleeding, rashes, swelling, wound problems and problems with drains and lines, while protecting dignity and preventing heat loss. Hidden bleeding or a rash can be missed in an alert patient. Problems found earlier in ABCD are treated as you find them, never delayed until E.

questions.title: Deterioration case: suspected opioid toxicity

competency.objective: Recognise respiratory failure and arrest and act accordingly:

references.supports: Manage airway and breathing, give oxygen and call for help in a patient with reduced consciousness and respiratory depression.
Naloxone is the antidote used to reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression (BNF naloxone monograph).

fields.stem: An adult using a morphine patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump after surgery is found responding only to pain. Respiratory rate 7 breaths/min, SpO2 89% on room air, pupils pinpoint.

parts.prompt: (a) What is the most likely cause?
(b) What are your immediate actions?
accepted: Call for help, open the airway, give high-flow oxygen and support breathing with a bag-valve-mask if needed, and stop the PCA
Emergency call, airway and breathing support with oxygen, stop the PCA

parts.prompt: (c) Which medicine reverses the cause, given as prescribed or per local protocol?

keyPoints: Pinpoint pupils, low respiratory rate and reduced consciousness point to opioid toxicity
Call for help, open the airway, give oxygen, support breathing, stop the PCA
Naloxone as prescribed or per protocol, then monitor because it can wear off before the opioid
misconceptions: Wait for the doctor before supporting the airway
Leave the PCA connected because the patient needs pain relief

fields.rationale: Reduced consciousness, a respiratory rate of 7 and pinpoint pupils in a patient on a morphine PCA suggest opioid toxicity. Call for help, open and support the airway, give oxygen, assist breathing with a bag-valve-mask if needed, and stop the PCA. Naloxone, given as prescribed or under the local protocol, reverses opioid effects; it can wear off before the opioid does, so keep monitoring closely.

questions.title: Deterioration: first response to an unresponsive patient

competency.objective: Can describe how to call for help in cardiac arrest situation

references.supports: In-hospital: check response, shout for help, open the airway, look listen and feel for breathing and pulse for no more than 10 seconds, call the resuscitation team if no signs of life, start CPR 30:2 and attach a defibrillator as soon as possible.

fields.stem: You find an adult patient collapsed in bed on the ward. Put your first actions in the correct order.
steps: Check whether the patient responds and shout for help
Open the airway with head tilt and chin lift
Look, listen and feel for normal breathing, and check for a pulse, for no more than 10 seconds
If there are no signs of life, make sure the resuscitation team is called
Start chest compressions at 30:2 and attach the defibrillator as soon as it arrives

keyPoints: Check response and shout for help
Check breathing and pulse for no more than 10 seconds
Start CPR and attach the defibrillator
misconceptions: Start compressions before opening the airway and checking breathing
Spend as long as needed feeling for a pulse

fields.rationale: Check for a response and shout for help, open the airway, then look, listen and feel for normal breathing (and a pulse, if trained) for no more than 10 seconds. If there are no signs of life, make sure the resuscitation team is called, start compressions at 30:2 and attach the defibrillator as soon as it arrives. Follow your hospital's emergency number and procedure.

questions.title: Prioritisation: four patients at the start of a shift

competency.objective: Justifies a decision made under uncertainty by documenting options, foreseeable consequences, consultation and the point at which further help is required.

references.supports: Airway and breathing problems are life-threatening and take priority.
Low oxygen saturation and raised respiratory rate are high-scoring signs of deterioration.

fields.stem: At handover you are given four patients. Put them in the order you should see them, most urgent first.
steps: A patient with a new respiratory rate of 30 breaths/min and SpO2 88% on 4 L/min oxygen
A patient 2 hours after surgery with a pain score of 8 out of 10, observations otherwise stable
A patient due a scheduled oral antibiotic dose in 30 minutes
A patient waiting for discharge paperwork

keyPoints: Severe pain next: it causes harm and can mask deterioration
misconceptions: Patients are seen in bed order
A scheduled task always comes before a clinical concern

fields.rationale: Prioritise by threat to life: the patient with a rising respiratory rate and low saturation despite oxygen is deteriorating (A/B problem) and is seen first. Severe uncontrolled pain is next. A dose due in 30 minutes can be planned around the first two, and discharge paperwork can wait. In practice, escalate the first patient and ask for help if you cannot reach the others in time.

questions.title: Prioritisation: which patient first

competency.objective: Justifies a decision made under uncertainty by documenting options, foreseeable consequences, consultation and the point at which further help is required.

references.supports: Airway obstruction is assessed and treated before breathing, circulation and disability problems.

fields.stem: Four patients need you at the same time. Which patient should you go to first?
options: A patient with gurgling breathing who responds only to pain
A patient with heart rate 112 beats/min and blood pressure 105/70 mmHg after a fluid bolus
An alert patient with a blood glucose of 3.6 mmol/L who is eating breakfast
A patient with a temperature of 38.3 C who is shivering

keyPoints: Gurgling with reduced consciousness is an airway threat
Airway comes before breathing, circulation and disability
Ask for help with the others
misconceptions: The most abnormal number decides priority

fields.rationale: Gurgling breathing in a patient who responds only to pain means the airway is at risk from secretions or vomit, which can kill within minutes; it comes first in the ABCDE order. The others all need attention soon: the alert patient with low glucose is already eating, and the tachycardic and febrile patients should be reassessed as soon as possible or delegated to a colleague.

questions.title: Delegation: tasks for a healthcare support worker

competency.objective: Explains which responsibilities may be delegated in the current role and which accountability remains with the delegating nurse.

references.supports: Delegate only tasks within the other person's competence, make sure they are supervised and supported, and confirm the outcome meets the required standard; the delegating nurse remains accountable for the decision to delegate.

fields.stem: A healthcare support worker is trained and competent in the tasks below, and the patients concerned are stable. Which tasks can a registered nurse appropriately delegate? Select all that apply.
options: Recording a set of observations on a stable patient and reporting them to the nurse
Helping a patient with personal hygiene
Measuring and recording fluid intake and output
Assessing a newly deteriorating patient and deciding whether to escalate
Interpreting a NEWS2 score of 6 and deciding the clinical response

keyPoints: Delegate defined tasks within the worker's competence, for stable patients
Assessment, interpretation and clinical decisions stay with the registered nurse
The nurse stays accountable for the decision to delegate
misconceptions: Once delegated, the nurse is no longer accountable
Interpreting an early warning score is a routine task

fields.rationale: Recording observations, helping with hygiene and recording fluid balance are defined tasks that a competent support worker can do for stable patients, reporting back to the nurse. Assessing a deteriorating patient and deciding the response to a NEWS2 of 6 need a registered nurse's clinical judgement. The nurse remains accountable for the decision to delegate and for supervising the outcome.

questions.title: Clinical reasoning: concern despite a low NEWS2

competency.objective: Recognises the patient with abnormal neurological findings, including subtle changes in neurological status and escalates appropriately.

references.supports: New confusion scores 3; clinical concern by staff or family should prompt escalation regardless of the aggregate score.
A full ABCDE assessment, including blood glucose, for a patient with altered consciousness.

fields.stem: An older adult's NEWS2 at 10:00 was 2. At 11:00 their daughter tells you: 'Dad's not himself. He's usually sharp, but now he keeps asking where he is.' Explain how you would respond and justify each step.
fields.modelAnswer: Take the daughter's concern seriously: she knows his baseline. New disorientation is new confusion, which scores 3 on its own in NEWS2, so his score is now at least 5 and must be recalculated with a full set of observations. Perform a full ABCDE assessment, including SpO2, respiratory rate and a capillary blood glucose, and look for causes such as hypoxia, sepsis, hypoglycaemia, pain, urinary retention or medicines. Escalate to the medical team using SBAR on the basis of the new confusion and your concern, whatever the number, increase the frequency of observations, and document the change, the escalation and the plan.
keyPoints: Family concern about a change from baseline is a valid cue
New confusion scores 3 in NEWS2: rescore with a full set of observations
Full ABCDE assessment including SpO2 and capillary blood glucose
Escalate using SBAR on clinical concern regardless of the aggregate

misconceptions: A low earlier score means the patient is safe
Confusion in an older adult is expected and not significant

fields.rationale: New confusion is an early sign of deterioration (for example hypoxia, sepsis or hypoglycaemia) and scores 3 in NEWS2 on its own. A relative's concern about a change from baseline is an important cue. Reassess fully with ABCDE, rescore, escalate on concern whatever the number, and document.

questions.title: Prioritisation case: two alarms in one bay

competency.objective: Can recognise and respond in a timely manner when a patient requires: Supplemental oxygen, suction, nebulisers or repositioning

references.supports: For patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure the target is 88-92%; if saturation falls below target, increase oxygen within the prescription (for example a 24-28% Venturi mask), obtain a blood gas and seek medical review.

fields.stem: In your bay: Patient 1 has COPD with a prescribed target saturation of 88-92%. Their SpO2 is now 86% on 2 L/min via nasal cannula, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, alert. Patient 2's intravenous antibiotic pump is alarming 'occlusion'; they are comfortable with normal observations.

parts.prompt: (a) Which patient do you attend first, and why?
accepted: Patient 1, because their saturation is below the target range and they are breathless
Patient 1: hypoxaemia below target with a raised respiratory rate

parts.prompt: (b) What do you do for that patient?
accepted: Increase oxygen within the prescription to reach 88-92%, sit them up and escalate for medical review and a blood gas
Titrate oxygen to 88 to 92%, escalate, request arterial blood gas

parts.prompt: (c) How do you manage Patient 2 safely?
accepted: Ask a colleague to check the line and cannula, or check it yourself once Patient 1 is safe
Delegate or attend after Patient 1: check for a kinked line or closed clamp

keyPoints: Patient 1 first: saturation below target with tachypnoea
Increase oxygen within prescription to 88-92%, escalate, blood gas
Patient 2's occlusion is not immediately life-threatening: delegate or attend next
misconceptions: The loudest alarm is the priority
Hypoxaemia does not matter in COPD

fields.rationale: Patient 1's saturation is below their prescribed target and they are tachypnoeic: an A/B problem that comes first. Increase oxygen within the prescription to bring saturation back to 88-92% (avoiding both hypoxaemia and excessive oxygen), sit them up and escalate for medical review and a blood gas. The occlusion alarm on Patient 2's pump is not immediately life-threatening: ask a colleague to check the line or deal with it next.

questions.title: Clinical reasoning case: low urine output after surgery

competency.objective: Recognises deviations from normal hydration status and escalates concerns in a timely manner

references.supports: Indicators that a patient may need fluid resuscitation include heart rate above 90, capillary refill longer than 2 seconds or cold peripheries, systolic BP below 100 and NEWS 5 or more.
Urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour is a warning sign in catheterised adults.

fields.stem: Day 2 after surgery, a catheterised adult weighing 80 kg has passed 20 mL/hour for 3 hours. Heart rate 105 beats/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds, dry mouth.

parts.prompt: (a) Is this urine output acceptable? Explain using the patient's weight.
accepted: No, it is below 0.5 mL/kg/hour, which is 40 mL/hour for 80 kg
No, the minimum for 80 kg is 40 mL/hour

parts.prompt: (b) Which other findings support a problem with fluid status?
accepted: Tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill and a dry mouth
Heart rate 105, capillary refill 3 seconds, dry mucous membranes

parts.prompt: (c) What do you do next?
accepted: Check the catheter is not blocked or kinked, escalate to the medical team, and keep an accurate fluid balance
Check catheter patency, escalate for review and fluid assessment, hourly urine output

keyPoints: Tachycardia, capillary refill over 2 seconds and dry mouth suggest hypovolaemia
Check the catheter, escalate, monitor hourly
misconceptions: Low urine output is normal after surgery
The catheter cannot be the cause

fields.rationale: For 80 kg the minimum is 0.5 x 80 = 40 mL/hour, so 20 mL/hour for 3 hours is low. Tachycardia, capillary refill of 3 seconds and a dry mouth suggest hypovolaemia. First check the catheter is not kinked or blocked, then escalate for medical review and fluid assessment, continue hourly urine output and keep an accurate fluid balance.

calculation.rounding: whole number (exact here, no rounding applied)

questions.title: Clinical reasoning: the clinical reasoning cycle

competency.objective: Justifies a decision made under uncertainty by documenting options, foreseeable consequences, consultation and the point at which further help is required.

references.supports: The clinical reasoning cycle: consider the patient situation, collect cues, process information, identify problems, establish goals, take action, evaluate outcomes and reflect.

fields.stem: Put the stages of the clinical reasoning cycle in order.
steps: Consider the patient situation
Collect cues and information
Process the information
Identify the problem or issue
Establish goals and take action
Evaluate the outcome and reflect

misconceptions: Act first, then work out the problem
Evaluation is optional once action is taken

fields.rationale: The clinical reasoning cycle moves from considering the patient's situation and collecting cues, through processing them and identifying the problem, to setting goals and acting, and ends by evaluating the outcome and reflecting. It is a cycle: evaluation often sends you back to collect more cues.

questions.title: Escalation: when the first escalation is not acted on

competency.objective: Checks whether an escalated concern was acted on and re-escalates unresolved risk through the next appropriate route.

references.supports: An aggregate of 7 or more needs an emergency response by a team with critical care competencies.

fields.stem: 45 minutes ago you escalated a patient with a NEWS2 of 6 to the ward doctor, who has not yet arrived. The score is now 7. What should you do?
options: Escalate again through the next route, such as the senior doctor, nurse in charge, critical care outreach or emergency team, and document it
Wait, because the doctor has already been informed
Repeat the observations in 4 hours
Ask the patient's family to phone the doctor

keyPoints: An unanswered escalation is an unresolved risk
A score of 7 needs an emergency response
Re-escalate through the next route and document times and names
misconceptions: Once escalated, responsibility passes to the doctor

fields.rationale: Escalation is not complete until someone acts. The patient is deteriorating and now meets the NEWS2 emergency threshold of 7, so escalate again through the next route your hospital uses (senior doctor, nurse in charge, critical care outreach or the emergency team), stay with the patient, monitor continuously and document who you called and when.

questions.title: Deterioration: the NEWS2 threshold for possible sepsis

competency.objective: Understands the importance of recognising the signs and symptoms of infection, escalating appropriately and taking action

references.supports: An aggregate score of 5 or more is the key threshold for urgent response and should prompt consideration of sepsis in a patient with known or suspected infection.

fields.stem: In a patient with known or suspected infection, what NEWS2 aggregate score is the key threshold that should prompt urgent review for possible sepsis? Give the number.

keyPoints: Consider sepsis if infection is possible
misconceptions: Sepsis is only considered at a score of 7

fields.rationale: NEWS2 identifies an aggregate of 5 or more as the key threshold for urgent response. In a patient with known or suspected infection it should prompt urgent assessment for sepsis. Sepsis can be present at lower scores, so clinical concern still counts.

questions.title: Clinical reasoning: when NEWS2 alone can mislead

competency.objective: Is aware of the SBAR tool to support clear communication and other tools associated with clinical escalation such as early warning systems

references.supports: NEWS2 is not validated for children under 16 or for pregnant women; physiological responses may be modified by medicines such as beta-blockers, and clinical judgement takes precedence.

fields.stem: In which situations is a NEWS2 score LESS reliable as the only basis for a clinical decision? Select all that apply.
options: The patient takes a beta-blocker that limits how much their heart rate can rise
The patient is pregnant
The patient is 14 years old
A complete set of observations was recorded on time
The observations were recorded by a trained healthcare support worker
The score was calculated automatically by the electronic chart

keyPoints: Medicines such as beta-blockers can blunt the response
NEWS2 is not for use in pregnancy
misconceptions: NEWS2 applies to every patient
An automatic score cannot mislead

fields.rationale: NEWS2 was developed for non-pregnant adults aged 16 and over; pregnancy and childhood need age- or pregnancy-specific tools. Medicines such as beta-blockers can hide a rising heart rate. Who recorded the observations, or that the chart added them up, does not make the score less valid if the observations are accurate. In every case, clinical judgement and concern still drive escalation.

questions.title: Clinical reasoning: interpreting an arterial blood gas

competency.objective: Able to identify and demonstrate basic understanding of the causes of Respiratory Acidosis

references.supports: Hypercapnia is a PaCO2 above 6.0 kPa; respiratory acidosis is pH below 7.35 with a raised PaCO2; type 2 respiratory failure is hypoxaemia with hypercapnia.
Normal arterial values: pH 7.35-7.45, PaCO2 4.7-6.0 kPa, PaO2 above 10 kPa on air, bicarbonate 22-26 mmol/L.

fields.stem: An adult's arterial blood gas on room air shows: pH 7.28, PaCO2 8.2 kPa (61.5 mmHg), PaO2 7.6 kPa (57 mmHg), bicarbonate 25 mmol/L. Answer each part with one or two words.

parts.prompt: (a) Is this an acidosis or an alkalosis?
(b) Is the cause respiratory or metabolic?
(c) Which type of respiratory failure is this?

keyPoints: Raised PaCO2 with normal bicarbonate: respiratory cause
Low PaO2 with high PaCO2: type 2 respiratory failure
misconceptions: A low pH always means a metabolic problem
Any low PaO2 is type 1 failure

fields.rationale: pH 7.28 is below 7.35, so this is an acidosis. The PaCO2 is high (above 6.0 kPa) while bicarbonate is normal, so the cause is respiratory and not yet compensated. PaO2 is below 8 kPa with a raised PaCO2, which is type 2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure. Escalate urgently; oxygen should be given to a target of 88-92% while awaiting review.

questions.title: Clinical reasoning: acting on a subtle trend

competency.objective: Recognises changes in haemodynamic status and responds in a timely manner

references.supports: For scores of 1-4 the registered nurse decides whether to increase observation frequency or escalate; trends and clinical concern matter as well as the aggregate.

fields.stem: A patient with a NEWS2 of 1 tells you she feels 'something awful is going to happen'. Her heart rate has risen from 78 to 94 beats/min over 2 hours; respiratory rate is 20 breaths/min. What is the best next action?
options: Do a full ABCDE assessment now, increase observation frequency and escalate if the concern or trend continues, documenting what you find
Reassure her and repeat observations in 12 hours, because the score is low
Give her a sedative to settle her anxiety
Wait until the score reaches 5 before doing anything further

keyPoints: A sense of impending doom and a rising heart rate are cues of possible deterioration
Reassess fully and increase observation frequency
Escalate on concern or trend, and document
misconceptions: A low score means no action is needed
The patient's feeling is only anxiety

fields.rationale: A patient's sense of impending doom and a steadily rising heart rate are cues that can come before the score rises. Reassess with ABCDE now, increase the observation frequency, escalate if the concern or trend continues, and document. Sedating her could hide deterioration, and waiting for a threshold wastes time.

questions.title: Medication safety: confirming patient identity

competency.objective: Demonstrate effective use of technology and standardised practices that support safety and quality; effectively uses strategies to reduce risk of harm to self and others.

references.supports: Use at least two identifiers (for example name and date of birth), never the room or bed number, and involve the patient in identification.
Confirm the identity of the patient before administering a medicine.

fields.stem: Before giving a medicine to an alert adult, how should you confirm their identity?
options: Ask them to tell you their full name and date of birth, and check these against their identity band and the prescription
Read out the name on the chart, ask 'Is that you?' and check the bed number
Check the name written above the bed
Ask a colleague who knows the patient

keyPoints: Ask an open question: the patient states their name and date of birth
Check at least two identifiers against the identity band and prescription
Never use the bed or room number
misconceptions: A closed 'Are you...?' question is enough
The bed number identifies the patient

fields.rationale: Use at least two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, stated by the patient in answer to an open question, and check them against the identity band and the prescription. Patients may answer 'yes' to a closed question by mistake, and beds and signs change; neither is an identifier.

questions.title: Medication safety: unsafe ways of writing doses

competency.objective: Can describe human factors and other basic safety design principles; delineate general categories of errors and hazards in care, causes of error and allocation of responsibility and accountability (e.g. RCA); describe factors that create a culture of safety

references.supports: Guidance on prescribing: avoid unnecessary decimal points (3 mg not 3.0 mg), use a leading zero for values below 1 (0.5 mL not .5 mL), do not abbreviate micrograms, nanograms or units.
Write 'units' in full; abbreviations such as 'U' or 'IU' have caused tenfold insulin overdoses.

fields.stem: Which of these ways of writing a dose on a prescription are UNSAFE and should be queried with the prescriber? Select all that apply.
options: Insulin 10 U
Warfarin 5.0 mg
Colchicine .5 mg
Levothyroxine 25 micrograms
Morphine 2.5 mg
Insulin 10 units

keyPoints: 'U' can be misread as 0: write units in full
A trailing zero (5.0) can be misread as 50
A missing leading zero (.5) can be misread as 5
misconceptions: A trailing zero makes a dose more precise and safer

fields.rationale: '10 U' can be read as 100, '5.0 mg' as 50 mg and '.5 mg' as 5 mg, each a tenfold error. Safe practice is 'units' in full, no trailing zero and a leading zero before a decimal point. '25 micrograms' (written in full), '2.5 mg' and '10 units' are written safely. Query any unclear prescription before giving the medicine.

questions.title: Medication calculation: tablets

competency.objective: Demonstrate effective use of technology and standardised practices that support safety and quality; effectively uses strategies to reduce risk of harm to self and others.

references.supports: Metformin is available as 500 mg tablets; 1 g = 1000 mg.
Number of tablets = dose prescribed / strength of one tablet, with units converted first.

fields.stem: Prescription: metformin 1 g orally. Stock: metformin 500 mg tablets. How many tablets will you give? Give a whole number of tablets with the word 'tablets'.

misconceptions: 1 g is 100 mg
Divide the tablet strength by the dose

fields.rationale: Convert to the same unit first: 1 g = 1000 mg. Then dose / strength = 1000 mg / 500 mg = 2 tablets. If a calculation gives an unusual number of tablets, stop and check with a colleague or pharmacist before giving the medicine.

calculation.rounding: whole tablets (exact here, no rounding applied)

questions.title: Medication calculation: oral liquid

competency.objective: Demonstrate effective use of technology and standardised practices that support safety and quality; effectively uses strategies to reduce risk of harm to self and others.

references.supports: Amoxicillin oral suspension 250 mg/5 mL; adult oral dose 500 mg three times daily.
Volume = (dose prescribed / stock strength) x stock volume.

fields.stem: Prescription: amoxicillin 500 mg orally. Stock: amoxicillin oral suspension 250 mg in 5 mL. What volume will you give? Give your answer in mL as a whole number, with its unit.

misconceptions: Give 2 mL because 500 / 250 = 2
Give 5 mL because that is the stock volume

fields.rationale: Volume = (what you want / what you have) x the volume it is in = (500 mg / 250 mg) x 5 mL = 2 x 5 mL = 10 mL. Measure it with an oral syringe or a graduated measure, never a household spoon.

calculation.rounding: whole number (exact here, no rounding applied)

questions.title: Medication calculation: injection volume

competency.objective: Demonstrates knowledge of different types of common diuretics and their actions

references.supports: Furosemide injection 10 mg/mL.
Volume = (dose prescribed / stock strength) x stock volume.

fields.stem: Prescription: furosemide 40 mg intravenously. Stock: furosemide injection 10 mg/mL. What volume will you draw up? Give your answer in mL as a whole number, with its unit.

misconceptions: Divide the strength by the dose (0.25 mL)
Give 40 mL

fields.rationale: Volume = (40 mg / 10 mg) x 1 mL = 4 mL. Check the calculation independently with a second competent person where your policy requires it for intravenous medicines, and give IV furosemide at the rate stated in your local policy or the product information.

calculation.rounding: whole number (exact here, no rounding applied)

questions.title: Medication calculation: micrograms to millilitres for adrenaline

competency.objective: Familiar with the whereabouts and purpose of other emergency equipment such as the anaphylaxis box, difficult airway trolley, spill kit

references.supports: Adult intramuscular adrenaline for anaphylaxis: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL adrenaline), repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement.

fields.stem: An adult with anaphylaxis needs intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms. Stock: adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1 in 1000). What volume will you give? Give your answer in mL to one decimal place, with its unit.

misconceptions: 500 micrograms = 5 mg
Give 5 mL

fields.rationale: 1 mg = 1000 micrograms, so 500 micrograms = 0.5 mg. With 1 mg in each mL, 0.5 mg is 0.5 mL. Give it intramuscularly, ideally into the anterolateral thigh, and repeat after 5 minutes if there is no improvement. A tenfold error here is dangerous, so convert units before calculating.

calculation.rounding: one decimal place (exact here, no rounding applied)

questions.title: Medication calculation: infusion pump rate

competency.objective: Can administer fluid replacement of losses as prescribed and clearly document

references.supports: Infusion pump rate (mL/hour) = total volume (mL) / time (hours).

fields.stem: Prescription: 1000 mL sodium chloride 0.9% intravenously over 8 hours via a volumetric infusion pump. At what rate do you set the pump? Give your answer in mL/hour as a whole number, with its unit.

misconceptions: Divide by minutes when the pump is set in mL/hour

fields.rationale: Rate = volume / time = 1000 mL / 8 hours = 125 mL/hour. Check the pump settings against the prescription, confirm the volume to be infused, and check the infusion and the cannula site regularly.

calculation.rounding: whole number (exact here, no rounding applied)

questions.title: Medication calculation: gravity drip rate

competency.objective: Can accurately calculate daily and hourly fluid requirements and document clearly for infant/child/adult.

references.supports: Drops per minute = (volume in mL x drops per mL of the giving set) / time in minutes.

fields.stem: Prescription: 1000 mL sodium chloride 0.9% intravenously over 8 hours. No pump is available, and the gravity giving set delivers 20 drops per mL. Calculate the drip rate in drops per minute, rounded to the nearest whole drop, with its unit.

misconceptions: Divide by 8 hours instead of 480 minutes
Always round down

fields.rationale: Drops per minute = (1000 mL x 20 drops/mL) / (8 x 60 minutes) = 20000 / 480 = 41.67, which rounds to 42 drops per minute. Count the drops for a full minute when setting the rate and recheck regularly, because gravity infusions change with position and height of the bag.

questions.title: Medication calculation: weight-based intravenous paracetamol

competency.objective: Can demonstrate ability to identify the correct choice of analgesia taking into consideration non-pharmacological measures.

references.supports: Intravenous paracetamol for adults weighing 50 kg or less (BNF band 33-50 kg): 15 mg/kg per dose, maximum 60 mg/kg daily; paracetamol infusion 10 mg/mL.

fields.stem: Intravenous paracetamol is prescribed at 15 mg/kg for an adult who weighs 42 kg. Stock: paracetamol 10 mg/mL solution for infusion. Answer each part with its unit.

parts.prompt: (a) What dose is this, in mg as a whole number?
(b) What volume contains this dose, in mL as a whole number?
(c) Why must the weight be checked before giving intravenous paracetamol to a low-weight adult?
accepted: A standard 1 g dose would be too much for a low-weight adult and could cause liver damage
To avoid overdose and liver toxicity in adults of 50 kg or less

keyPoints: A fixed 1 g dose would exceed the weight-based dose and risk liver toxicity
misconceptions: Every adult gets 1 g
Give 630 mL

fields.rationale: Dose = 15 mg/kg x 42 kg = 630 mg. Volume = 630 mg / 10 mg per mL = 63 mL. For adults weighing 50 kg or less, intravenous paracetamol is dosed by weight; giving a standard 1 g dose would be about 24 mg/kg and risks liver toxicity, particularly if repeated. Check the weight, the maximum daily dose and the time of any earlier paracetamol from any route.

calculation.rounding: whole numbers (exact here, no rounding applied)

questions.title: Medication safety: order of the administration checks

competency.objective: Demonstrate effective use of technology and standardised practices that support safety and quality; effectively uses strategies to reduce risk of harm to self and others.

references.supports: Before administering: check the prescription, the patient's allergy status and identity, the medicine and dose against the prescription; record the administration promptly.
Medicine administration procedure and the sequence of checks.

fields.stem: Put these steps for giving an oral medicine on a ward round in a safe order.
steps: Check the prescription is complete, legible and current, and check the patient's allergy status
Prepare the medicine, checking its name, strength, dose, route and expiry against the prescription
At the bedside, confirm the patient's identity against their identity band and the prescription
Give the medicine and make sure it has been taken
Record the administration on the chart straight away

misconceptions: Sign the chart before giving the medicine
Identity can be checked after the medicine is given

fields.rationale: Start with a complete, current prescription and the allergy status, prepare the medicine against the prescription, confirm the patient's identity at the bedside before giving it, observe it being taken, and record it straight away. Never sign before giving, and never leave medicines unattended.

questions.title: Medication safety case: reaction during an antibiotic infusion

competency.objective: Describes commonly used medications in cardiovascular emergency, reasons for use and how to administer

references.supports: Recognise anaphylaxis (airway, breathing or circulation problems, usually with skin changes), call for help, remove the trigger, give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms in adults, position flat with legs raised or sitting if breathing is difficult.

fields.stem: During an intravenous antibiotic infusion, an adult develops widespread hives, lip swelling and wheeze. Blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg.

parts.prompt: (a) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(b) What do you do with the infusion?
accepted: stop the infusion and keep the cannula

parts.prompt: (c) What is the first-line medicine, its adult dose and route?
accepted: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL)

parts.prompt: (d) How do you position the patient?
accepted: lying flat with the legs elevated
flat, legs raised, or sitting up if breathing is difficult

keyPoints: Hives, lip swelling, wheeze and hypotension after a new medicine: anaphylaxis
Call for help and stop the infusion
IM adrenaline 500 micrograms, repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement
Lie flat with legs raised (sit up if breathing is difficult)
misconceptions: An antihistamine is the first treatment
Sit a hypotensive patient upright

fields.rationale: Skin and lip swelling with wheeze and hypotension after starting an IV antibiotic is anaphylaxis. Call for help, stop the infusion (keep the cannula), and give intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) for an adult, repeating after 5 minutes if there is no improvement. Lie the patient flat with legs raised, or let them sit up if breathing is difficult; give high-flow oxygen and IV fluids as directed. Antihistamines are not first-line. Document and report the reaction and record the allergy.

questions.title: Medication safety: drawing insulin from a pen device

competency.objective: Can describe human factors and other basic safety design principles; delineate general categories of errors and hazards in care, causes of error and allocation of responsibility and accountability (e.g. RCA); describe factors that create a culture of safety

references.supports: Insulin must never be withdrawn from pen devices or cartridges with a syringe: some pens contain higher-strength insulin (for example 200 or 300 units/mL) and insulin syringes are graduated for 100 units/mL, risking severe overdose.
Insulin doses are measured only with an insulin syringe or pen device.

fields.stem: The pen needles have run out, and a colleague suggests drawing a patient's insulin out of their pen cartridge with an insulin syringe. What is the main danger?
options: The pen may hold a higher-strength insulin than the 100 units/mL the syringe is marked for, causing a large overdose
Insulin is inactivated as soon as it touches the plastic of a syringe
The only risk is that the cartridge is no longer sterile for the next dose
Insulin syringes cannot measure doses below 20 units

keyPoints: Never withdraw insulin from a pen or cartridge with a syringe
Some pens contain 200 or 300 units/mL, but syringes are marked for 100 units/mL
Get pen needles or a vial supply through pharmacy; do not work around the device
misconceptions: All insulin is 100 units/mL
A workaround is acceptable if the dose is checked

fields.rationale: Insulin syringes are graduated for 100 units/mL insulin, but some pens contain higher-strength insulin (for example 200 or 300 units/mL). Drawing from a pen with a syringe can therefore give two or three times the intended dose and cause severe hypoglycaemia. Never withdraw insulin from a pen or cartridge; obtain pen needles or an appropriate supply through pharmacy and escalate if a dose will be delayed.
